entries.title: Every remote operation runs async, and local-only fabric pairs stay an explicit choice only
entries.brief: Remote work goes async except the branch-exists check; batch pairs reach origin like any pair, and the local-only mode stays only as an explicit --local until a use is found or it is removed
entries.body:
## Seen

`batten-start-speed` builds local-only fabric pairs (`fabric add --local`, a local-only branch mark in `gitrepo` with a push refusal, pushes that skip such branches, and local modes of `fabric remove` and `fabric cleanup`): about 630 lines of code, 1360 with tests, plus a local-mark check in the status-push spawn entry.
The mode came from an orch recommendation in `weaver` that batch pairs never reach origin, which was wrong: a batch pair's commits are part of the implementation, and an agent continuing the work on another machine must see what a batch left half done.
The time it saves is small: in the sandbox hub `lym fabric add` took about 1.1 s, nearly all of it two synchronous `git ls-remote` origin probes, with local work about 50 ms and its push already async; `lym fabric remove --remote` took 6 to 7 s of network, at teardown, where nothing waits on it.

## Decisions (operator, 2026-10-18)

- The local-only pair mode stays for now, only as an explicit `fabric add --local` choice, since local work that needs no remote (experiments, local testing) may use it; no lym flow creates local pairs, batch pairs included.
  Remove it (`--local`, the local-only branch mark and its push refusal, the skipped-local reporting in pushes, the local modes of remove and cleanup, and the local-mark check in the status push) if no use turns up.
- Every operation against a remote runs async, so no lym command waits on the network.
  This includes `fabric remove`'s 6 to 7 s of network at teardown (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete).
- One exception may stay synchronous: the check whether a pair's branches already exist on origin, since a branch found there is fetched and the work continued on, and that is worth waiting for.
  Today that is `fabric add`'s `git ls-remote` probes; they may run in parallel to cut the wait.

## Open

- Which remote operations are synchronous today besides `fabric remove`'s (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete); an audit of the call sites belongs to the task that builds this.
- How an async remote failure reaches the operator or the orch.

entries.title: Plan writer cost: sub-planners per part, and twill versus a solo writer
entries.brief: The Plan writer is 18% of spend; sub-planners per part for large bundles, and a twill versus solo Opus high comparison on cost, rounds and time
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: the Plan writer is the costliest session type, about $8 per run, $1,306 with its forks over two weeks (18% of all spend).
It averages 81 turns at a mean context of 223k, holds 153k by its first fork and peaks around 308k, mostly from about 71 raw `sed -n`/`grep` code reads.
Every `twill-plan` lens fork inherits that context, about 287k per turn; since 2026-10-20 the writer and its forks cost about $18 per run.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Fork the lenses earlier, before the code reads pile up, or hand the writer a digest of the code it needs instead of raw reads.
Cutting a quarter of the writer's and its forks' cost saves about 4.5% of all spend; quality must be benched first.

## Discussion with the operator (2026-10-22)

- A code digest instead of raw reads is rejected: it is too inexact unless the code itself is read, and the writer would read the source anyway to be sure.
  Finding what to read is already `relevant.md`'s job; whether the writer uses it is worth measuring (how much of what the writer read the list named).
- Lens forks as fresh agents are rejected: that is the perch itself.
- Sub-planners: Discussion splits the scope into parts in the decision record, groups `relevant.md` per part, and each sub-planner reads only its part; the lead owns the shared spots and joins the card DAG.
  This keeps every review round and matters more as loom tasks are bundled larger.
  Review could split per part the same way, since each fresh reviewer rebuilds its context every round (Plan reviewer: 48 turns at 123k mean context, $2.48 per session).
- Twill-plan versus a solo writer: since the full `twill-plan` fan (2026-10-20), 7 landed loom runs average 2.00 Plan rounds against 2.09 before, while the writer's forks cost about $7 per run and a Plan round about $3.70; too few runs to judge.
  The operator sees strong signs that the twill writer makes a far better one-shot plan in shorter time, and time counts as well as tokens.
  Still, test a solo Opus high writer: compare twill, solo Opus high and solo Fable on Plan cost, Plan rounds and Plan wall time (`lym report timing`) per run.

## Split writing: two variants to bench (operator, 2026-10-22)

Discussion-Write and Plan-Write already run as `shedadapters.MultiLLMProducer` over a `seatengine` table, a chair and advisors; advisors only advise, and twill is the chair forking itself, so today one session writes the whole product.
Two ways to have parts written separately, both benched against each other and against the twill and solo writers before anything reaches production:

1. **Seats with writing assistants.** The chair splits the scope, fixes the interfaces and shared spots, and hands each assistant seat its part; it then joins and checks the parts.
   A new seat role beside the advisor.
   Risks: assistants see neither each other's work nor a shared context, so seams fall to the chair and review, and overlapping parts make several seats read the same code.
2. **Fork-based.** The chair keeps its context lean (scope, split and shared spots only) and forks once per part, so every part writer inherits the same overview without the writer's full reading.
   Technically still one writer with forks, like twill but forking early.

## Data check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

Plan writer plus its lens forks, means per run (API list price):

| group | runs | writer+forks | forks | Plan-Write wall | Plan rounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before 10-15 (solo writer) | 28 | $9.08 | $0.58 | 16.4 min active | 1.3 |
| 10-15 to 10-19 | 41 | $9.39 | $3.86 | 18.5 min | 1.88 |
| 10-20 to c62274be5 (full twill-plan fan) | 7 | $18.14 | $7.66 | 23.9 min | 2.00 |
| after c62274be5 (five lenses) | 3 | $16.64 | $7.40 | 23.9 min | 1.33 |

- The later groups are larger tasks, so the cost rise is not the fan alone; the five-lens group is too small to judge.
- `relevant.md` use, over 32 runs with a list and a Plan-Write transcript: 85% of named files were read, but only 28% of read files were named (about 3.5 files read per file named, about 7 on large runs). Both shares are lower bounds (directory greps and quarry reads not counted).
- So `relevant.md` works as a floor, not a boundary; most unnamed reading looks like tests and neighbouring callers, which a per-part split of the list would not remove.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench; the split-writing variant has since been built and benched against `Plan-Write` (see the last section).
- Scripts, baseline tables and `results.md` are in `docs/research/plan-writer-audit-2026-10-24/`; rerun per its README.

## Discussion versus Plan: double reading (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-25)

55 loom runs seeded 2026-10-15 or later with both a `ly:<slug>:discussion` and a `ly:<slug>:plan` transcript on this machine; cost at API list price from the 10-24 tokencount reports, per run:

| | Discussion | Plan |
|---|---|---|
| phase total (writer, forks, review, fix) | $8.68 | $18.51 |
| writer session alone | $2.07 | $6.60 |
| writer turns / mean context | 39 / 89k tokens | 83 / 183k tokens |
| repo files read by the writer (pooled) | 1,093 | 3,286 |
| share read by both | 62% of Discussion's reads re-read by Plan | 21% of Plan's reads read by Discussion |
| same, without `PATTERN.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `pattern/`, `docs/` | 64% | 20% |

- Discussion costs 0.47 of Plan for the phase and 0.31 for the writer alone; Discussion was the dearer phase in only 4 of 55 runs.
- Plan-Write re-reads about 62% of the files Discussion-Write read (mean of per-run shares 62%), so exploration is repeated, but Plan reads about three times as many files and most of its reading (79%) is new.
- Rough size of the repeat: the Plan-Write reads that Discussion had already made are about 3.3M tokens pooled, about 59k per run (file bytes at current `main` divided by 4; whole files assumed, so an upper bound).
  That is roughly a third of the Plan writer's mean context, and it is paid again on every later turn through the cache.
- File-level only: directory greps, globs and `lym quarry` reads are not counted, and a file is the same file by path, not by the lines read.
- The Discussion phase total holds its review rounds and fixers, which is most of its cost beyond the writer; the segment figures come from the 10-24 tokencount reports, so runs landed since are priced as of then.
- Rerun: `.scratch/discussion-overlap/reads2.sh <slug> plan|discussion` per run, then `analyze.sh`; both stay in `.scratch` and are not committed.
- Decision (operator, 2026-10-25): Discussion stays a separate step; folding it into the Plan writer would add turns to the costliest session.

## Turn audit (landed 2026-10-28)

`docs/research/turn-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` (n = 1 loom run, 213 sessions) finds the Plan writer spends 33 of its 101 turns on serial single-call reads and searches, mostly shell `grep` and `sed -n`, which a merged turn would remove.
It recommends one stencil sentence in `loom-template-plan.md` and in the twill lens directive: issue every search and read you can name in one message.
This is a cheaper cut than the digest, the earlier fork and the split writing above, and the audit proposes no pre-read for the writer.
The Plan row rests on one session; the recommendation was later applied and measured, see the next section.

## Batching effect audit (landed 2026-11-01)

The turn audit's recommendation above was applied (the batching sentences of `bf00a043`, 2026-10-28), and `docs/research/batching-effect-audit-2026-11-01/report.md` measured it on 8 runs, 7 landed (5 before, 2 after).
It finds no batching effect, and the sample cannot show a small one: the Plan writer issued 1.14 calls per turn after against 1.29 before, its single-call turn share was 83% against 75%, and its serial read and search turns were 44% of its turns against 41%.
The Discussion writer is level on every measure.
The 33-of-101 serial turns the turn audit found are still there, so the ideas above keep their value.

## Batching moved to heddle (landed 2026-11-01)

`plan-edits-before-gate` (`1834cebf`) removed the batching sentences from the stencils, `loom-template-plan.md`, `loom-template-discussion.md` and `twill-directive.md` among them.
The one rule (read in one message, decide every edit, make them in one message, one gate run) is now the shipped heddle entry `lym-plan-edits-before-gate`, rendered after `lym-batching`.
Its effect on agent behaviour is not measured; `agent-turns-effect` measures it.
`plan-reviewer-batching` (`5227aeaa`) added a wave structure for the fanned Plan reviewer's pre-read in `burler-fork-reading.md`; it too is unmeasured.

## Split writing built and benched (landed 2026-11-01)

The second variant above exists as two opt-in producers: `Parts-Write` splits the task into parts with contracts and shared spots, and `Parts-Plan-Write` runs one fresh writer session per part under a joining chair.
Both sit behind the tapestry flag `plan_split` (off by default; `Plan-Write` stays the default), and the joined plan passes the ordinary `plan` gate.

`plan-split-bench` (`989a8b85`, `docs/research/plan-split-bench-2026-11-01/`) benched them against `Plan-Write` on replays of `warp-visibility` and `run-verbs-shared`, one Plan-Review round each.
- `warp-visibility`: the split cost $16.69 against $14.93 and took 15m39s against 25m07s; its largest session peaked at 245k context against 408k.
  The split plan had 34 cards against 15 and its review found 4 blocking findings against 3.
- `run-verbs-shared`: the plan arm cost $28.03 with a 674k peak; the split arm failed when reed lost the chair strand (note `reed-loses-parts-chair`), so there is no comparison.
- The joined split plan passed its gate only after two hand edits to `parts.md`, both defects of `Parts-Write`; the report recommends keeping `plan_split` off.
  Task `plan-split-tune` tunes the split writers on this.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench, and a repeat of the split bench after the tuning.

## Data point: `cold-gate-fixer` Plan-Write (orch, 2026-11-02)

One loom run, read from the writer's transcript and its subagents' by a read-only agent; the numbers are the writer's own context, by last turn usage.

- The writer made 45 tool calls in about 25 turns before it started `fork0`: 22 Reads (18 whole-file, 4 slices), 16 Bash calls (about 14 single lookups, 2 `cat` of whole files), 5 Agent calls and 2 skill loads.
- The writer followed the Sonnet-subagent rule: five read-only `general-purpose` agents with `model: sonnet`, launched together at 115k context.
  Each ended at 39k to 73k and ran 33 to 61 seconds; their answers added little to the writer.
  The 115k they were started at had already come from the writer's own whole-file Reads and `cat`s, so the subagents did not keep the reading out of the writer's context.
- `fork0` (Opus) started at 198k, inherited it, ran 17 minutes and ended at 338k; the writer was at 204k when it returned.
- After `fork0` returned, the writer read all 14 plan files back in one batch, 35k tokens (205k to 240k), the largest jump of the later phase.
  The five lens forks then started at 243k and added 2k to 20k each; the lens fixes, 8 more files and 24 edits in a row took the writer to 332k.
- The phase took about 31 minutes: exploration about 3, `fork0` 17, lens review about 3, and about 5 idle waiting on `validate-plan` and the lens forks.
- No compaction and no threshold event fired.

Reading: the writer must read much to write a joined plan, and `fork0` gets that reading for free by inheriting it, so the cost is the 198k each fork carries, not the reading itself.
Two cuts remain open: have the first exploration fan answer with the lines needed (sonnet reads, writer gets excerpts) instead of the writer reading whole files after it, and skip the read-back of every plan file when `fork0` has already validated them.

### Correction (operator, 2026-11-02)

The second cut above, skipping the read-back of the plan files after `fork0`, is rejected.
The read-back is needed: the writer gets the plan from `fork0` without `fork0`'s reasoning, so it must read the plan to judge it, and the lens forks then review a plan whose reasoning nobody carries, which makes them the more critical check.
Only the first cut (excerpts from the exploration fan instead of whole-file Reads by the writer) stays open.

entries.title: Plan and Discussion fixers on Sonnet, once findings are concrete enough
entries.brief: Webster and Merge fixers are already Sonnet; Plan and Discussion fixers need concrete findings first
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: Opus and Sonnet read cache at the same price, so a swap saves about half a role's non-cache-read cost.
Over the audit window the Plan and Discussion fixers cost about $162 on Opus, the darn writer $45, alignment $40.
The Webster and Merge fixers already run on Sonnet: the template sets `webster_fixer_model` and `merge_fixer_model` to `sonnet[medium]` since `c2d13e5ae` (2026-10-21), so the audit's $37 Opus Webster fixer spend predates that.
`discussion_fixer_model` and `plan_fixer_model` are empty and fall back to `fixer_model`, `opus[medium]`.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-22)

A Sonnet fixer needs findings concrete enough for Sonnet to carry out.
For the Webster perch Sonnet is the natural fit, since Webster's own forks are Sonnet.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Before the Plan and Discussion fixers move to Sonnet, check that their findings are concrete: each names the place and the change, not only the problem.
A3 (`review-setup-audit`) notes a sloppy fixer causes many late-round defects, and `docs/research/model-downgrade-results.md` holds earlier downgrade results; bench before switching.

## Review-setup audit (landed 2026-10-28)

`docs/research/review-setup-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` is the A3 audit named above.
It does not measure fixer quality or a model swap.
Its finding that bears here: in Plan round 3, 14 of 23 findings point at cards the round-2 fixer left alone, so those late defects are the writer's repository-invariant misses and not a sloppy fixer's; the audit recommends `validate-plan` checks for them.

## Machine checks landed (task `validator-checks`, 2026-10-28)

`lym loom validate-discussion` and `validate-plan`, and the gates that call them, now refuse the recurring findings a machine can see: decision ids and acceptance coverage, missing cited paths and symbols, and in plans `seam-test-unlisted`, `test-tier-unstated` and `doc-go-unlisted`.
That is the audit's recommended `validate-plan` step, so the writer's repository-invariant misses are caught before a review round; the fixer-quality question here is unchanged and still needs a bench.

entries.title: A run keeps the lym binary and Bolt instructions it started with
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run reads its instructions live while it runs: the `lym` binary, and the stencils, specs and hub config on Bolt (`_bolt/_lym/{stencils,specs,config}`).
A landing deploys a new `lym` and can change those files, so a run started on one version can finish on another, such as a darn run that sat between its drift rows when `darn-drift-await-row` landed and its recipe changed under it (that landing wrote no transition code: such a run halts at Drift-Verify and is settled by hand with `lym drift waive`).
LoomYard takes no special care for such a run today, and the operator wants none written per change (operator, 2026-10-27).

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run keeps the version it started with, so nothing changes under it.
- Bolt: the run records the Bolt commit at its start and reads stencils, specs and config from that commit through git, in the one place those files are read, instead of from the working files; no copy is made.
- Binary: at the run's start the running `lym` is copied into a store under a name derived from its content, as the gate's prebuilt store does (`internal/gateslot`), and the run's driver and agents call that copy.
- Shared state stays live: the board, locks, gate slots, creel mail and the run's own records.
- One verb moves a run onto the newest version, for a run that needs a fix that landed after it started.

## Open

- Shared daemons (dobby, creel, gate) run the newest binary, so a pinned run's formats must stay readable by them, and a pinned binary must not write the board in an older format.
- Plugins and skills are loaded by Claude Code from one shared place and are left out of the first step.

entries.title: Creel mail between hubs through an inbox folder, with a verified sender
entries.brief: A shared inbox folder takes mail from other hubs; each file names the sender hub and agent so a reply knows where to go
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

The operator sometimes has the orch write straight into another repository, such as Scribe or Quarry, and would rather let the orchs of the hubs talk to each other, which is how lym is meant to be used.
Creel has no support for this today.
One daemon serves one hub, its socket is named from the hub path, and the hub a call reaches is the hub of the directory it runs from.
A process outside the hub's strands is `EXTERNAL`, shown with a terminal and parent-process envelope, and its replies reach only a waiting `post --wait-reply`.
`EXTERNAL` is the wrong sender for this: the receiver must see the real strand that sent the message.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-30)

A shared inbox folder takes in messages from outside the hub.
The file a message becomes carries its sender: the path of the sender hub's inbox folder and the name of the agent that sent it.
A message needs a receiver, so the daemon knows whom to give it to.
A reply is addressed from those two fields, so the replier knows which agent in which hub to answer.

## Verifying the sender (operator, 2026-10-30)

A file cannot prove its sender: any process of the same user can write one, so a prompt-injected agent could write `ly:orch` in the sender field.
The sending daemon, which reads the caller from `SO_PEERCRED` as it does today, writes the file.
The receiving daemon then asks the sending hub's daemon to confirm it:

1. The file names the sender hub's path, and the receiver derives that hub's socket name from it, as `creel-<shortname>-<hash>.sock`, with no registry.
2. The receiver sends one call in creel's JSON-lines protocol, such as `confirm`, with the message id, the receiver and a hash of the text.
3. The sender's daemon looks in its own journal for a message from that strand to that receiver with that hash, and answers yes or no, never the text.
4. Only on yes does the receiver show the sender as that strand; otherwise the message shows as unverified.

This is a call and not a signature on the file, since a signature needs a secret and every agent of the same user can read a secret file; the sending daemon cannot be fooled, because it reads its caller from the process and knows what it sent.
A message can be confirmed once, so a copied file cannot be reused.
The journal's retention bounds how late a confirmation can come, so the receiver confirms when the message arrives.
A sending daemon that is down is started as a client starts it today, or the message stays unverified.
The check works only within one user, since the sockets do.

## Open design points

- Where the folder lives and how a sender addresses a hub: a path derived from the hub path, like the socket, and a record on the machine that maps a shortname to a hub path.
- What a reply does across the hub border: it goes to the sender's inbox folder, addressed to the agent the file names.
- How a role treats mail from another hub: as data to weigh, never as the operator's instruction, since it is a channel for prompt injection into the receiving orch.
- How this fits a closed area for lym's process tree (research note `sandboxing-options-2026-10-30`): the folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.
- Another machine: a folder that a synced directory carries would reach a hub on Neve; not designed here.

entries.title: A closed area for lym: bwrap sandbox in stages, off by default
entries.brief: Run the lym process tree in a bwrap area with a host proxy and broker, built in three stages with a stop; to be split if it goes ahead
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

Every agent lym starts runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which many people do not accept, and a repository that states it supports safe sandboxing is worth more than one that does not.
The operator uses lym alone, on Linux (OSL-1046: Ubuntu 24.04; Neve: Kubuntu on Ubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6), and has no interest in other users or in Windows.
The research is `docs/research/sandboxing-options-2026-10-30.md`: it weighs `bwrap`, Landlock, a dedicated Linux user, systemd sandboxing, podman and Claude Code's own `/sandbox`, and the packages and cards each would change.

Two exposures hold today with no area: an agent can reach `/run/user/<uid>/bus` and through it `systemd-run --user`, which starts any process outside lym's tree, and it can type into other hubs' tmux panes through their sockets in `/tmp/tmux-<uid>`, the Models hub's among them.

## Idea

Run the whole lym process tree inside a `bwrap` area launched by lym itself, with the agents free inside it and a short, controlled list of exits.
It is an option the operator turns on, never a requirement: with it off, everything works as it does today, and with it on, nothing starts when the sandbox cannot.
The operator thinks the full design is complicated and error-prone, and doubts it will work without large problems, so it is built in stages with a stop between them.
This is one large note and is split into tasks, or a project, only when the operator decides it goes ahead.

### Before the area: two cheap steps

- Start a hub's tmux server from a Konsole window, not a VS Code terminal: the server inherits the `vscode` AppArmor profile, which grants user namespaces to every agent of the hub.
- A line in `README.md` that every agent lym starts runs with bypass permissions, and that lym belongs on a machine the operator is willing to hand to its agents.

### Stage 1: the filesystem area only

`bwrap` with `--unshare-all --die-with-parent --clearenv` around reed's tmux server and everything under it, started by a new `lym area start` and a supervisor inside.

- The hub is bound read-write at its own path, since the tmux server name, the creel socket name, git's worktree links and Claude Code's transcript directory all derive from absolute paths; `/usr`, `/etc` and `/opt` are read-only, `$HOME` a tmpfs with read-only binds of the Go toolchain, the Claude Code binary and the installed `lym`.
- The area has its own Claude config directory and Go caches bound at the usual paths, with the host's plugin cache read-only on top, so the host's `settings.json` hooks never run in it.
- One host directory holds the tmux socket directory, so `lym reed attach` from outside drives the server inside; tried on OSL-1046 with a tmux server inside `bwrap`.
- `.git/hooks` is read-only; `.git/config` stays writable, since `internal/gitrepo/branchmark.go` writes `branch.<b>.lymLocal` into it.
- Network stays open and there is no broker, so the landing deploy, `lym reed window`, `lym ide` and `lym hibernate request` do not work from inside; the operator does them by hand, from outside.
- A config module `area` with `required`, off by default; `lym area start` refuses on any failure and never falls back to an unsandboxed start.
- Ubuntu 24.04 needs a one-time AppArmor profile for `/usr/bin/bwrap`, loaded by root; the report names the profile, and Ubuntu 25.04 and later ship it, which is not verified on Neve.

This closes the two exposures above and shows early whether tmux, creel and dobby run well inside an area.

### Stop: the operator decides whether stage 1 works well enough to go on.

### Stage 2: egress through a host proxy

No network inside the area; a host-side proxy, reached through a bound socket, allows CONNECT to `api.anthropic.com`, `claude.ai`, `platform.claude.com`, `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`, `github.com` and `api.github.com`, with a loopback relay inside the area.
Telemetry and the auto-updater are off by environment.
The GitHub token handed to the area is fine-grained and limited to the hub's repositories; the operator's `gh` login never enters.
WebFetch and the `prowler` skill reach only these hosts.

### Stage 3: a broker for the remaining exits

A host-side process serving a fixed set of verbs and never a command line from the area: the landing deploy (it fetches `origin/main` into its own clone, checks the commit is the tip, builds with the host's Go and installs), `lym reed window` opening Konsole, and `lym hibernate request`.
`lym ide` is refused, since VS Code on the host would run git over repositories the area writes; the host runs no git over the area's repositories at all.

## What is not claimed

Isolation from a kernel exploit, which needs a virtual machine; that data in the area cannot leave through an allowed host; and that a landed change of lym itself cannot run on the host once deployed, which matters on this hub because it develops lym.
Landlock stays a possible inner layer once both machines run a kernel with ABI 9 and 10, and Claude Code deny rules in shuttle's settings are a cheap second line inside the area; the dedicated user, podman, systemd sandboxing and Claude Code's `/sandbox` inside lym runs are left out.
The report estimates the whole at five tasks and eighteen cards.

## Related

Note `creel-cross-hub-mail`: the inbox folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.

entries.title: Merge in from parent as a task of its own in a beam, before pawl lands it
entries.brief: A command on a beam files a merge-in-from-parent task, run as darn with its perch on
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

The pawl recipe, a beam's run, had a Code-Review perch of its own; the operator did not want it, since the beam's members are already reviewed by their own runs.
The perch is gone: pawl became a loom recipe with no review round (`pawl-loom-recipe`), and Parent-Align brings the parent in before Finalize and Beam-Down land the beam.
Nothing now checks that a beam has reached its project's goal before it lands: Beam-Await ends on a land request.

## Idea

Bringing the parent into a beam is a task of its own: a run with its own worktree inside the beam's project, "merge in from parent".
- It runs as darn with its perch on, not with review off (operator, 2026-11-01).
- A command on the beam, such as `lym beam merge-parent <beam>`, files such a task in the beam's project with one call, at any time, not only at landing; dobby starts it as any member (operator, 2026-11-01).
- The run merges the parent into the beam, settles conflicts and gate failures with the merge fixer, and can run Drift.
- pawl lands the beam without a perch round of its own (built by `pawl-loom-recipe`).

## Open

- The command's name.
- Whether its perch also reviews the beam against the project's decision record, so this is where the project's goal is checked before the beam lands.
- Whether pawl starts such a run itself before it lands, or requires one to have landed since the parent last moved.

entries.title: An idle interactive run saves its work and pauses, to go on another time

## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

An interactive run (the `sampler` recipe, landed by task `interactive-recipe`) waits for the operator in its pane at the `Sampler-Session` row, and has dobby's quiet notice and the step watchdog off while it does.
The row waits with no timeout until the agent runs `lym loom sampler-done` at the operator's word.
Since lym runs the agent, it can watch how long the agent has waited.

## Idea

When the agent has been idle for a set time, lym asks it to write down what it has, commit it, and end its session; the run pauses, and the operator picks it up another time with the agent resumed from that state.

`lym hibernate request` runs a daemon of its own that waits for the runs to land and every session to pause before it hibernates the machine.

entries.title: Comment cleanup: parallel agents fix stale comments across the repository
entries.brief: An orchestrating agent hands each package to a worker, possibly Haiku 5.5, that fixes comments no longer true or pinning perishable specifics
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-31)

Comments in the Go source go stale as the code moves on.
Two found today: `internal/fabricengine/weftwiring.go` still speaks of a future `_lym/raddle/` squash-merge-back, though raddle will never be built; and many comments spelled the `_board` path instead of naming its constant (the rename to `_bolt` in `bolt-dir-rename` has since replaced the spelling itself).
There are surely more, in every package, against `scribe:prose`'s rule never to pin a perishable specific.

## Idea

A comment-cleanup campaign over the whole repository.
- A worker fixes each comment or text that no longer matches the code, names something gone or planned and dropped, or pins a perishable specific: a count, a list of current callers, a path or name spelled where a constant or identifier should be named.
- Workers change comments and text only, never code.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-31)

- One darn run, whose agent orchestrates the whole campaign: it splits the work and spawns the workers, many in parallel; not one darn per package, which would be far too many runs.
- Scope: Go comments and docstrings, each package's `doc.go`, the stencils and the docs.
- Models by scope: Haiku 5.5 takes the comments and docstrings of code files, being fast and cheap while its context stays under about 100k, which one package's read fits; `doc.go`, stencils and docs need a stronger model, Sonnet 5.5, as the `docs` profile's writer is.
- No review step of its own: most comments are assumed sound, and this run is itself the check on them; the darn's usual Code-Review is enough.

Related: note `hardener` is another autonomous campaign run by an orchestrating agent.

## Open

- How the orchestrating agent spawns its workers under lym, with Haiku 5.5 as their model.

entries.title: A status-bar button opens a short-lived board agent, so board talks need no orch
entries.brief: An ordinary agent with a board-policy skill loaded, for discussing and filing notes and releasing tasks on go-ahead
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

Adding, changing or removing board entries is done today by talking to the orch, a long-lived session that carries every run's notices, escalations and rules, which is heavy for a talk about one or a few notes.

## Idea

A reed status-bar button of its own, added to the configurable action buttons reed now ships (`reed.yaml` `buttons`, landed 2026-11-01: one config entry per button, no build), opens a short-lived agent for board work.
- The button opens an ordinary agent, as `lym shuttle open` does, with a skill loaded that makes it a board agent; no new role, so the same way can make other kinds of agent later (operator, 2026-10-31).
- The agent reads the board and the code it needs, talks one or a few cases through with the operator, writes, merges or removes notes, promotes notes to tasks and releases tasks on the operator's named go-ahead (operator, 2026-10-31), and exits.
  The board holds its state, so it needs no handoff and no context cycle.
- `ly:board` holds the mechanics of the board only; the policy, today the orch role's "The board" section (one finding per note, discuss before writing, a body holds the current design only, propose bundles and wait for approval, release only on a named go-ahead), moves into a skill of its own that the button loads and the orch role points to, so the policy lives in one place.
  It does not go into `ly:board`, which run agents load to file notes.


## Splitting an entry

The agent can also split an entry into tasks, as the first of the ways note `discussed-task-split` describes.

## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

The orch is a long-lived, heavy session that handles board work, run notices and escalations alike.
Board work can move to a short-lived board agent (note `board-agent-button`), and dobby already does the mechanical run work.

## Idea (long term)

Dobby takes everything mechanical, and a capable agent spawned per case, as the arbiter is for a halted stop, settles the doubtful ones.

entries.title: A landing notice is not lost when set late, when dobby was down, or when the orch is absent
entries.brief: Close the known limits landing-watch left: a late notify_on_land, a Land passed while dobby was down, and a dropped line when no orch is live
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-01)

`landing-watch` (commit `c9d52bdb`) has dobby send the orch a line when a task with `notify_on_land` set lands.
Its commit lists known limits that no note covered:
- A `notify_on_land` set after the run passed Land gets no line.
- A run that passes Land while dobby is down long enough for a fresh state record to be written gets no line.
- The line needs a live orch; after three failed posts it is dropped.

The commit also records that the notice was never run end to end against a live orch.

## Open

- Whether any of these matter in practice, and which to close (operator to look at them).
- Setting the field on a run already past Land could answer at once instead of staying silent.
- A dropped line could wait in creel for the orch rather than be lost, which fits the dormant orch in `dormant-orch`.

entries.title: The decision record on the board, and splitting a discussed task
entries.brief: A task flagged discussed carries its decision record on the board and skips Discussion; three ways to split, from by hand to stitch
entries.body:
## Seen

A task's decision record lives only in its run's weft (`_lym/discussion/decision-record.md`): a cancelled run leaves it in the records history, and no new task takes it along.
So when Discussion finds a task too large, or the operator decides a tapestry run should rather be split, what Discussion found is lost or must be copied out by hand.
Several notes circled the same question (where the decision record lives, how a task is split); this note joins them.

## Core: the decision record on the board (operator, 2026-11-01)

- When Discussion is approved, after its review, the decision record is copied into the task's board entry, and the entry is flagged as discussed.
- A task flagged discussed skips Discussion: tapestry starts at Plan from the record, and darn takes the record as final, as darn takes its task text as already discussed today.
- Changing one's mind loses nothing: the run is cancelled, the record stays on the board, and it can be split into discussed tasks or made a project.
- lym itself writes the record field, at Discussion's approval and at each `lym loom decision add`, so the field is exempt from the lock on a claimed entry.
  That lock exists only so the orch does not change a task's text after its agents have read it; a record written by lym is not that.

## Ways to split, simplest first

1. The operator, or the board agent of note `board-agent-button`, splits a discussed entry into tasks with `depends_on`, each with its part of the record and flagged discussed.
   The same agent can split an undiscussed entry before it runs, but then each part runs its own Discussion and rereads much of the same code; a tapestry part carries about $23 of fixed cost, so this pays best when the parts are darn-sized.
2. Discussion finds the task too large or proposes a split: it writes its findings and the proposed parts into the record, tells its parent and ends its turn.
   It files no task or project and starts nothing; the operator decides, and the parts become plain tasks in the prime or, for a large one, a project and beam spawned from the parent, never from the old task's worktree.
   Its prompt must hold back: one part is the default, a split only where the seams are clear and each part pays for its own Plan and review, and small parts go to darn.
3. `stitch`: a stand-alone loom recipe for a large task's whole course, chosen before the run starts.
   Preflight, Discussion, a Pre-Plan producer that splits the decided scope into parts with contracts (what each takes in, delivers and exports, and which parts it depends on), a row with no agent that turns the entry into a project and files each part as a darn task, then an inner pawl run through `battenshed.NewInnerRun` that brings up the beam, waits until every part has landed and lands the beam.
   Parts run with review off; one review covers the whole diff after the last lands.
   It is tried first as a hand-run test project with the projects and beams that exist, measured against tapestry runs of the same size (`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`), and built only if it saves tokens.
   The risk: tapestry's build is cheap because Webster runs on Sonnet following an Opus plan, while parts under a coarse pre-plan likely need Opus writers.

## Open

- Where the records live: in `board.json`, or in a file of their own in the Bolt checkout beside it with the same entry-level replay, since a record is often 10–30 KB.
- A split record's format: each part must still pass the discussion check.
- Whether the old run's commits, if any, are kept when a run is cancelled for a split.
- `stitch`: contract precision, how large the whole-task review's fixes may be, and how often the choice between `stitch` and tapestry before the run is right.

entries.title: A module overlap lets a task run Discussion at once and wait only before Plan
entries.brief: A second kind of dependency, plan_after: the task starts and discusses, then waits before Plan until the named tasks have landed
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-01)

Two tasks that share a module label are chained with `depends_on` today, so the later one waits for the earlier to land before it starts at all, Discussion included.
Finer labels or file-level overlap checks after Plan were weighed and rejected: what a task touches is unknown until it is planned, two plans made at once against moving code do not match, and pausing runs before Webster by what they planned is too complex.
Only Discussion can usefully run alongside; planning must be done against code that does not change under it.

## Idea

A second kind of dependency beside `depends_on`:
- `depends_on`, as today: the task does not start until the named entries land; for a real dependency, where Discussion needs the other's result.
- `plan_after`: the task starts and runs Discussion at once, then waits before Plan until the named tasks have landed; for tasks that only share a module.
- The overlap notice of `set-deps` and the upsert verbs proposes `plan_after` instead of `depends_on`.
- For darn, which has no Discussion or Plan of its own, `plan_after` acts as `depends_on`.

## Waits on

Note `discussed-task-split` first: the decision record on the board, so a discussed task waiting before Plan keeps its record where the board shows it (operator, 2026-11-01).

entries.title: The arbiter settles review escalations and records their decisions, so they never reach the orch
entries.brief: Decision escalations become eligible for the arbiter, and the arbiter may record decisions and accept or continue a review
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and orch, 2026-11-01)

Review escalations reached the orch four times in a few hours for `plan-split-producers` and `reed-status-buttons`, and the orch read each through a fork of its own session and recorded the answer with `lym loom decision add`, `lym loom circling accept|continue` and `lym loom resume`.
The calls were run-level: whether a fix in the record holds, whether to accept at the hard cap, small rulings inside the board entry's design.
The arbiter, a cold stronger-model agent the Go driver spawns at a stop it cannot settle (`internal/shedarbiter`), exists for such calls, but two limits sent them on:
- `internal/arbiterstop` makes only a review escalation of cause `hard-cap` or `circling` eligible; a `decision` escalation, such as a fixer's decision findings or a bouncer that wants the parent's ruling, goes to the run's parent without the arbiter.
- An eligible arbiter may only resume (a goto) or hand on: it records no decision and edits nothing.
  At `reed-status-buttons`' hard cap it found the false clause, wrote the exact three-line correction, and still had to hand on, since "I may edit nothing beyond this verdict, and no recorded operator decision covers it".

## Idea (operator, 2026-11-01)

The arbiter settles these calls itself, so they never reach the orch.
The chain stays as it is: the driver's rules, then the tackler, a cheap agent for mechanical stops, then the arbiter, a strong agent for judgment, and the parent last; a review escalation is a judgment call, so it goes to the arbiter, as it does today.
- A `decision` escalation becomes eligible for the arbiter as `hard-cap` and `circling` are.
- The arbiter may record a decision with `lym loom decision add`, under its own `--by`, and choose `circling accept` or `continue`, as the orch does today.
- The arbiter may make the one edit its stop asks for and nothing beyond it, such as the correction of a false clause in the decision record it has found; anything wider it records as a decision for the run's own agents to carry out.
- It passes on only a question the board entry's design and the record's decisions do not settle; that goes to the operator through the orch.
- The orch hears only the outcome, so a quiet orch, as in note `dormant-orch`, need not wake for it.

## Open

- How far the arbiter may decide alone: within the board entry's design and the record's decisions, and where that line is drawn in its stencil.
- Whether `--by arbiter` is a new decision author, shown as such in the record.

entries.title: A status-bar button asks for a value, so an agent opened from it gets a name
entries.brief: Button entries take ask, filling {answer}; the agent button asks for the strand name, and term becomes terminal
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-01)

The reed status bar's shipped `agent` button runs `lym shuttle open --role agent --model 'opus[high]'`, so every agent opened from it gets the strand name `agent`, and a second one only reed's number, `agent-2`.
With several agents each looking at its own thing, nothing in the strand name says which is which.

## Design (operator and orch, 2026-11-01)

- A button entry in `reed.yaml` (and `desktop.yaml`'s machine buttons) takes an optional `ask`, a prompt text beside `confirm`.
- A click on an entry with `ask` raises tmux's `command-prompt` on the clicking client with that text; the answer fills the placeholder `{answer}` in the entry's `run`, shell-quoted like the other placeholders, and the entry then runs as today, through `confirm` when it has one.
- An empty answer fills `{answer}` with the entry's `ask_default`, so a button still runs when the operator just presses Enter; an Escape cancels the click.
- `{answer}` is valid only in an entry with `ask`, checked where the other button rules are checked.
- The shipped `agent` buttons, in the POSIX and Windows templates, become `ask: "Agent name:"`, `ask_default: agent` and `run` with `--role {answer}`.
- The shipped `term` buttons are labelled `terminal` (operator, 2026-11-01).

entries.title: Measure the effect of the agent-turns project
entries.brief: Turns, calls per turn and cost before and after P2 agent-turns, for darn writers, Webster forks and review roles
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-11-01)

Measure the effect of project `agent-turns` as a whole, once its members have landed and runs have gone through with them, rather than one member at a time.

## Measure

- Baseline: the numbers in `agent-turns`' body (`tools/tokencount` and `tools/forkaudit` on `warp-visibility`, `interactive-recipe` and `run-verbs-shared`), and `docs/research/review-turn-audit-2026-11-01` for the review roles.
- After: the darn and tapestry runs that landed after the members, as many as there are; darns weigh most, since they run most.
- Darn writers: turns, calls per turn, shell edits against Edit-tool edits and gate-loop turns, with the scripts of `docs/research/turn-audit-2026-10-28`.
- Webster forks: turns per card, calls per turn and peak context, with `tools/forkaudit`; cost with `tools/tokencount`.
- Review roles: calls per turn, fork wake-up turns and removable turns, with the scripts of `docs/research/review-turn-audit-2026-11-01`.
  This includes `plan-reviewer-batching`, which has the fanned Plan reviewer gather its fork pre-read in parallel waves: count its pre-read turns against the baseline.
- Refused turns: the baseline is 6 turns refused by lym's guards across the five heaviest forks; count them again, and count `awk ... > file && mv` edits, the route the shell-edit guard leaves open.
- The report names which members' behaviour shows in the transcripts and states the sample size beside each number.

## Card gate fix loops (operator, 2026-11-01)

Before `agent-turns`, a Webster fork fixed its own card gate's failures in its own session, at 150k to 450k tokens of context a turn; one fork spent 69 turns in that loop.
Since then `gate-failure-report` gives one report listing every failure, and `plan-edits-before-gate` tells agents to fix everything a report shows in one message.
The report counts, per fork, the turns spent between a failing card gate and its next green one, and their tokens and peak context, beside the 69-turn baseline; the cold gate fixer itself is task `cold-gate-fixer`.

entries.title: Tune the plan-split writers until a split plan joins with no hand edit
entries.brief: Tune, replay on two inputs, tune again, at most 3 rounds, starting from the plan-split-bench report
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, plan-split-bench, 2026-11-01)

In the `plan-split-bench` replays, Parts-Write fixed export names in `parts.md` that the repository's PATTERN entries forbid, and the part writers, who may not change `parts.md`, could not correct them:
- `internal/heddlecli#NewCommand`, where `PATTERN-cli-cobra` gives every CLI package `Command()`;
- names spelling `warp` in `heddleengine`, `fabricengine` and `cmd/lym`, which `PATTERN-fabric-vocabulary` bars and `validate-plan --part` refuses as `fabric-vocabulary-name`;
- two members that keep their signatures listed as exports, which `part-export-missing` cannot accept.

Each needed a hand edit of `parts.md` before the parts could join.
Parts-Write's prompt (`loom-template-parts.md`) carries the PATTERN directive, but nothing has it read the PATTERN entries that govern the names it fixes, and its own gate does not run the name checks the part gate runs.

## Goal (operator, 2026-11-01)

Tune the instructions of the plan-split writers, Parts-Write, the part writers and the joining chair, test them, and tune again, until a split plan joins and passes its gates with no hand edit.
Start from the `plan-split-bench` report's findings, which this task reads first.

## Changes to try first

- Parts-Write reads the PATTERN entries for every package a part exports from before it names an export, as the Plan writer does in its longer session.
- Parts-Write's gate runs the name checks `validate-plan --part` runs on export names, `fabric-vocabulary-name` included, and refuses an export naming an existing member whose signature the part keeps, so such a defect stops at Parts-Write, where it can still be fixed.
- Whatever else the bench report names as a cause of a hand edit or a failed join.

## Loop and cap

- Inputs: the two replays `plan-split-bench` used (`warp-visibility` and `run-verbs-shared`), at the same base commits.
- One round: tune the instructions, then replay Parts-Write and Parts-Plan-Write on both inputs with `plan_split` on, and record per input whether the parts joined, which gates refused, and every hand edit needed.
- At most 3 rounds, so at most 6 split writings; one Plan-Review round per input on the last round's plans only, 2 in all.
- The loop ends early at the first round where both inputs join and pass their gates with no hand edit.
- The orch creates and removes the scratch worktrees on the writer's request, since `lym fabric add` is refused from a task session.
- The instruction changes land in the stencils and gates; a report in `docs/research/` gives each round's results and the cost.

entries.title: Fewer agent turns, fewer tokens
entries.brief: Token savings by cutting agent turns, above all late turns at large context

entries.title: Plan and Discussion writers explore through parallel Sonnet agents that return only what is relevant
entries.brief: Bench the guidance that sends Plan and Discussion writers' lookups to parallel Sonnet subagents against a writer given none
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-01)

In a sample of 28 sessions (`.scratch/batching-breach.md` of the batching study), the single largest cost was the Plan writer of `run-verbs-shared` in `plan-split-bench`: 31 chained grep turns at 390k to 530k context and 15 one-file-per-turn fix turns at 630k to 668k.
Every lookup the writer makes is paid at its whole context, so exploration late in a large session is the expensive part of planning.
Discussion-Write explores the code more than any other role, so the same cost applies there.

## What is being benched

The writers hand batches of independent lookups to fresh Sonnet subagents that return only what is relevant, with paths and line ranges, and read only what those lists name.
The writer is encouraged to work this way by its stencil, not commanded.
Task `explore-subagent-model` has landed (2026-11-02): the Discussion-Write stencil now carries the guidance the Plan and darn stencils already carried, and the subagent model is the `subagent_model` key of `loom.yaml` (default `sonnet`), read by all three stencils.
A fork does not serve for lookups: it inherits the writer's whole context and saves nothing.

## Research

- From the Plan-Write and Discussion-Write transcripts of landed tapestry runs, count the writers' exploration turns, their context and cost, and how many could have gone to parallel explore agents up front.
- Bench on one or two replays (the `plan-split-bench` inputs) for both roles: the writer allowed subagents but given no stencil guidance, against the writer with the guidance.
  Compare whether the guidance changes what the writer does, and cost, turns, peak context and review findings.
- Name the risk: an explore agent's list may leave out what the writer would have seen in the code, so count review findings that trace to a missed fact.

## What the bench writer did (orch, 2026-11-01)

The `psb-rv-plan` writer ran on `opus[medium]`; its Agent calls were one fork writing the plan and the `twill-plan` lens reviews, none for lookups.
No run denies the Agent tool any more, so a writer may start a fresh subagent.

## Timing

The guidance now exists for both roles, so the bench no longer waits on `explore-subagent-model`.
The "no guidance" arm needs the guidance removed from a stencil in the bench's own worktree, since the landed stencils all carry it.

entries.title: One cold, cheap fixer clears a failed writer gate instead of the writer at full context
entries.brief: When the Darn-Write, plan, discussion or Webster card gate fails, Go spawns one shared cold fixer with the gate report, generalised from webster fix-verify
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-01)

A writer that fails its own gate fixes the failures in its own session, at its full context per turn.
Before project `agent-turns`, one Webster fork spent 69 turns at 150k to 450k fixing its card gate.
The Plan writer runs `validate-plan` through its gate at 400k to 670k context in large runs, and the Discussion writer runs `validate-discussion` the same way.
The darn writer of `gate-one-binary-per-package` fixed its own `darn-write` gate failures at about 274k context, and darn is the recipe that runs most.
The gate reports name each failing check and its place, so most fixes are mechanical.

## Design (operator, 2026-11-01)

- One shared cold gate fixer, not four: when a writer's gate fails, Go spawns a fresh, cheap fixer with the gate report and the files it names, instead of the writer fixing in its large session.
  The fixer reads the failing source itself, fixes every failure in one go and reruns the gate, the failed packages first and then the whole gate; when it clears the gate the run goes on, and when it does not the failure goes back to the writer, or up the recovery ladder, as today.
- Webster's `lym webster fix-verify` (`webster-prefix-verify-fix-cold.md`), the cold fixer of the plan-level verify gate, is generalised into the shared one rather than built beside.
- Four callers:
  - the Darn-Write gate (`darn-write`);
  - the Plan writer's plan gate;
  - the Discussion writer's gate;
  - the Webster card gate, where Go spawns the fixer in the fork's worktree with the gate report, the card and the card's diff.
- Which failures the fixer takes: the failures a gate reports as machine checks go to it; a failure whose fix changes a design choice goes back to the writer. The Discussion settles the line from what the gate reports contain.
- The fixer's model and effort are config, one key per caller, with a cheap default; the Discussion picks the default.
- R1 (`agent-turns-effect`) measures the card gate loop after this lands.

entries.title: A task with no recipe runs darn, not tapestry
entries.brief: The default recipe becomes darn, set in board.yaml, so a small task promoted without a recipe does not start a full tapestry run
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-01)

A task with no recipe runs tapestry: `boardengine` reads an empty `recipe` as tapestry (`defaultRecipe` in `render.go`, the `Recipe` field comment in `task.go`), and the seeding site resolves it the same way.
A note promoted without a recipe, `plan-spec-split`, a rewrite of one markdown file, so started as a full tapestry run before the operator stopped it.
Darn is what most tasks need; tapestry is the exception for large or design-heavy work.

## Idea (operator, 2026-11-01)

- The default recipe becomes darn: a task with no recipe runs darn, and the README's Recipe column shows darn for it.
- The default is a hub setting in `board.yaml` (for example `default_recipe`), with darn as the template's value, so a hub can choose.
- The board skill, the CLI help and the docs that say "empty means tapestry" follow.
- Tasks already on the board with an empty recipe: the change names them, so the operator can set tapestry on any that need it before it lands.

entries.title: Finalize releases the parent lock while its fixer works
entries.brief: A red verify in Finalize frees the parent lock before the fixer starts, then requeues, merges and verifies again, so green runs land while one run fixes
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-01)

Finalize takes the parent lock (`landingshed/parentguard.go`) before it merges the parent in and verifies, and holds it through the whole row: verify, and on a red verify the fixer session and the re-verify.
`plan-spec-split` held the lock on `main` for 12 minutes: its first verify failed tier0, a fixer worked about 5 minutes, then the re-verify ran every tier.
Meanwhile four green runs queued behind it (`darn-sonnet-helpers`, `readme-profile-in-recipe-column`, `dobby-idle-notice-row-end`, `reed-loses-parts-chair`), each to verify under the lock in turn.

## Design (operator, 2026-11-01)

- Finalize keeps taking the lock before its merge and verify, so a run that verifies green lands what it verified, with no second merge.
- When verify fails, Finalize releases the lock before the fixer starts, so the next run in the queue can land meanwhile.
- When the fixer is done, the run queues for the lock again, merges the parent anew, and verifies under the lock as on its first try.
  When nothing landed on the parent while it fixed, that merge is a no-op and only the re-verify remains, which a red verify runs today too.
- Taking the lock only at the very end was weighed and rejected: the parent moves between the run's merge and its landing, so the run would merge, verify and fix again, and could starve while much lands.

## Hand-over latency (orch, 2026-11-01)

A queued run polls the lock from one second, doubling to thirty seconds while the holder is unchanged (`parentlock/acquire.go`), so after a long hold the next run takes the lock about 20 to 30 seconds after the release.
Two hand-overs on 2026-11-01 took 23 and 21 seconds (`plan-spec-split` to `darn-sonnet-helpers`, `dobby-idle-notice-row-end` to `reed-loses-parts-chair`).
The release wakes the head of the queue at once, through a notify on the lock directory or a lower poll ceiling of a few seconds.

## Open

- Whether a run that failed once goes to the back of the queue or ahead of runs queued while it fixed.
- How the wait mark and `lym loom status` show a run fixing outside the lock, and how the recovery ladder counts a second failed verify.

entries.title: The orch role explains how to make a project into a beam
entries.brief: The prime orch in the Models hub did not know beam create is the only way, and patched a plain task run by hand.
entries.body:
Seen in the Models hub: its prime orch could not make project P1 into a beam, because the orch role it follows never says how.

The role lists `lym beam create <slug>` in its command list and says a beam is "a project entry made a beam", but it holds no procedure, so the agent read a missing worktree as the fault and patched it by hand.

## What went wrong

- P1 was started as an ordinary task run (rows Worktree-Create, Seed-Child, …, Run-Shed) instead of a pawl run (Worktree-Create, Beam-Up), and the agent read only that the worktree was missing.
- It used `lym fabric add`, which only gave the wrong run a worktree back; a beam never comes of it.
- When lym refused, it tried `rm` on the directory itself instead of stopping to ask.
- The way out was `lym batten cancel` on the wrong run, then `lym beam create` from the prime.

## Design

Add a "Making a beam" section to `contracts/orchrole/orch-role.md`:

1. A beam is a board project entry that `lym beam create <slug>` turns into a beam: `lym board upsert` with `"kind":"project"` first, then `lym beam create <slug>`, run only from the prime or a parent beam, never from a task worktree.
2. The verb starts a batten run for the project whose Worktree-Create row makes the worktree, unmarked, and whose Seed-Child row seeds the inner pawl run in it; the pawl run's Beam-Up row marks the worktree a beam and starts the beam's own dobby and orch.
   The orch appears only after Beam-Up, so the operator attaches to a beam later than the create.
   A task run has the same batten rows but an inner tapestry or darn run, which has no Beam-Up, so it never becomes a beam.
3. `--anchor <dir>` gives the beam its own anchor; without it the beam inherits its parent's.
4. `lym beam start <slug>` brings an existing beam back up; it refuses a task pair, and never makes a beam.
5. A project that already runs as a task run is not a beam: `lym batten status <slug>` shows the rows, and the way forward is `lym batten cancel <slug>` with the operator's word, then `lym beam create`.
6. Never `lym fabric add`, and never delete a worktree directory by hand, to repair a run; when lym refuses, stop and tell the operator.

Fold the weakness behind issue #9 (a batten pass that fails forever when the worktree is gone) in only as a separate finding: its premise in the Models case was the wrong run kind, not the missing worktree.

entries.title: Measure the effect of the batching breach hook
entries.brief: After the batching breach hook lands, compare breach turns and context tokens against the 28-session baseline and tune its thresholds
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-11-02)

Measure over time whether the batching breach hook (task `batching-breach-nudge`, landed 2026-11-02) cuts the drift it targets, and tune its config thresholds from what is seen.

## The hook as landed

A PostToolUse hook on Read, Grep, Glob, Edit and Write runs `lym shuttle hook-batching claude <state file>` and adds one `additionalContext` line on a breach; it never denies.
It judges three breaches: a single-lookup chain, a Read slice, and an edit-only chain.
Its thresholds are the `batching_nudge` block of `claude.yaml`: `context_tokens` 150000, `lookup_run` 3, `edit_run` 2, `slice_lines` 2000, `max_nudges` 5, and an `enabled` switch beside one per breach.
A run copies the values at its start into a per-run `batching-nudge.json` beside its events file, with the nudge count, so a running session keeps the values it started with.

## Measurement

The baseline is the 28-session sample behind `batching-breach-nudge`: single-lookup turns that follow another single lookup above 150k context, 128 turns and 34.7M context tokens, and edits spread over consecutive turns, 39 turns and 15M, about a third of the sample's 147M.
Measure the same two figures, and the context tokens of every session, over a later sample of sessions with the hook on, with the transcript tooling under `tools/` (`tokencount`) extended where it lacks the breach counts.
Compare the two samples by recipe and role, since a darn writer and a plan writer drift differently.
Also read how often the hook fired and how often the next message after a firing batched, from the per-run `batching-nudge.json` nudge counts and the transcripts, and how many firings were on a lookup that had to be sequential.

## Bounds

No new agent run is made: the work reads the transcripts and hook state of sessions that already ran.
The later sample is taken at least two weeks after the hook landed, so not before 2026-11-16, with the hook's thresholds unchanged over that window.
It runs as darn with profile `docs` in its own worktree, so the report lands as a commit, and its report names any threshold change it recommends as a note of its own.

## Timing

The hook has landed; the work waits only for the later sample to exist.

entries.title: Beam orch cannot set a board entry's profile: refused as a task session
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #12](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/12).

Seen: in a beam's orch (strand mo:loomyard-setup:orch), `lym board upsert` with `"profile":"docs"` on a new task under the beam's project was refused: "a run_settings or profile change is refused from the task session mo:loomyard-setup:orch; way forward: the operator or the hub orch makes the change". The same upsert without `profile` succeeded, so the beam orch may create tasks but not set their profile.

Expected: the orch role tells every orch, a beam's included, to name a profile in the board entry's `profile` field before the batten run starts. A beam's orch (role `orch` under a beam slug) should be treated as an orch, not as a task session, for profile and run_settings writes on entries whose parent_beam is its own beam.

Workaround: created the task without a profile and asked the operator or the prime orch to set it.

entries.title: Two Claude accounts, each worktree on one of them by a configured weight
entries.brief: A claude config lists accounts with a config directory and a weight; a worktree picks one when its first session starts, so account A can carry twice the load of B
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-11-02)

Spread Claude usage over two accounts, so one account's limits are not the bottleneck: each worktree uses one of the accounts, chosen by a weight.
The weights are config, for example account A twice for each use of account B, so account A carries twice the load of B on average.

## Seen (orch, 2026-11-02)

Lym cannot do this today.
`lym config claude` has no key for an account, a config directory or an environment, and a search of `internal/` found no use of `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so every session runs under whichever account the machine is logged in to.

Claude Code is believed to keep an account's login in a config directory that the `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable selects.
That is not verified: check it against the Claude Code documentation before anything is built.

## Design questions for a Discussion

- Config: a list of accounts, each with a name, a config directory and a weight, in the claude config; a machine-layer key, since the accounts belong to the machine.
- Choice: per worktree, never per session, so all of a run's sessions (writer, reviewers, fixers, driver) share one account.
  The pick is made once, when the worktree's first session starts, and recorded with the worktree so a resume, a re-attach and a hand pass keep it.
  Candidates for the pick: a deterministic hash of the slug against the weights, which needs no state and never gives one slug two accounts, or a persisted counter that deals the accounts out in the weighted ratio, which keeps the ratio exact over a few runs.
- Scope: the prime's orch and each beam's orch and dobby need a rule of their own, since they outlive a task run.
- A session spawn sets the chosen account's environment in one place in the claude engine's launch, so no caller sets it.
- A usage limit on one account: whether lym moves a worktree to the other account when one is limited, or only reports it; the first needs the session's history to be readable under the other account, which it is not by default.
- Cost and quota reports (`lym report`, `tokencount`) read transcripts per config directory, and would need to read both.

## Not in scope

Logging the accounts in, and whether the use is within the accounts' and the organisation's terms, which is the operator's to settle.

entries.title: gitexec TestRun_RemoteBounds fails under machine load
entries.brief: The 200 ms stall bound of the never-answering remote test kills git before its ext script writes its count file when the machine is loaded
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-02, from the darn writer of `tmuxkit-short-socket-path`)

`gitexec` `TestRun_RemoteBounds/a_remote_that_never_answers...` sets a 200 ms stall bound.
At a load average of about 30, git is killed before its ext script writes its count file, and the test fails.
`heddle-render-ignores-anchor` failed the same way (gate log `20261102T135456Z-tier1-2983004`), and a rerun at `-count=1` by the writer of `tmuxkit-short-socket-path` failed the same way, although its change touches neither package.

## Idea

Make the test's bound independent of git start-up time, for example wait for the count file before the stall starts counting, rather than raising the number.
The writer reads the test and says what its 200 ms is meant to prove.

entries.title: The sampler agent gets no PATTERN directive
entries.brief: The sampler writes and commits code but its prompt carries no PATTERN directive, unlike every other code-writing role
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-02)

An interactive sampler agent told the operator that PATTERN reaches only the loom agents, not an interactive session: working directly with Claude in the code, it does not see the abscissa rule.

## Cause (orch, from the source)

`internal/samplerengine` and `contracts/stencils/sampler/sampler-template-agent.md` name no PATTERN directive, and the stencil's markers are `slug`, `task_worktree`, `decision_record_path`, `parent_directive` and `edit_directive` only.
Every other code-writing role renders `pattern.Directive` into its prompt: Webster (`internal/websterengine`), darn (`internal/darnengine/spec.go`), Drift-Verify (`internal/driftengine/seats.go`), the Discussion and Plan writers (`internal/loomengine`) and the review seats (`internal/burlerengine`).
The sampler is the one role that writes and commits code and gets none.

## Fix

Render the PATTERN directive into the sampler's prompt with `pattern.Directive`, as `VerifyTable` does for its implementer seat, and add a marker for it to the stencil; the role is `pattern.RoleImplementer`, since the sampler writes code today.
Add a test that the sampler's prompt carries the directive.
The directive is needed whatever the sampler's direction (note `sampler-direction`): should it become a read-only discussion role, only the role passed changes, to the Discussion writer's.

entries.title: A wake from hibernate leaves the hub-wide pause live
entries.brief: After waking, the hibernate request read done but its hub pause stayed live and held every network call; its wake notice failed on a wrong receiver and an oversized line
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-02)

Neve hibernated through `lym hibernate request` on 2026-11-01 at 21:03 and woke on 2026-11-02 at 19:02.
After the wake the request read phase `done`, yet `_bolt/.lym/pause/record.json` still held the hub-wide `hibernate` pause as live.
`lym hibernate cancel` did nothing, since the request was done, and `lym adopt root` sat with every network call held ("held by a hub-wide pause since 2026-11-01T21:03:00"), which looked like a hang to the operator.
The watcher's wake notice failed twice (`_bolt/.lym/hibernate/watch.log`): first the receiver `ly:orch` does not exist, then the notice line was 105 KB, over creel's 8 KB limit for one hook delivery.

## Workaround

The orch ran `lym tender resume`, which lifted the pause, and adopt went on.

## Expected

- The wake lifts the pause it added before anything else, and a failed notice never keeps it.
- The wake notice reaches the orch by its real creel name and stays a short line, with any long detail in a file it names.
- `lym hibernate cancel` on a done request still lifts a pause the hibernate left live.

entries.title: Operator verbs print a short readable summary, not a JSON dump
entries.brief: lym adopt root and other verbs the operator types print a long JSON envelope; print a short summary with each stop and its way forward by default, JSON behind a flag
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-02)

Operator-facing verbs such as `lym adopt root` print one long JSON envelope: on a stop it carries every commit hash of a divergence and every run's record, so the operator cannot see what happened or what to do next.

## Idea

- A verb the operator types prints a short human summary by default: what it did, what stopped, and the way forward for each stop, one line each.
- The full JSON envelope stays available behind a flag, for agents and scripts.
- Long lists, such as a divergence's commit hashes, collapse to a count with a pointer to where the full list is.
- Which verbs count as operator-facing follows the command index's operator audience.

## Open

- Whether agents call these verbs too, and so need the flag added to their stencils and skills.

entries.title: lym adopt root leaves the installed lym older than the adopted main
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-02)

Root moved back to Neve after a day of landings on OSL-1046.
The orch brought Neve's `loomyard` `main` level with origin and ran `lym adopt root`; neither step deploys, so `/home/knatte/go/bin/lym` stayed the binary built on 2026-11-01 from `87553450ec14`.
The weft and Bolt checkouts carry the new board stencils, while the binary is the old one.
The two darn runs released next, `plan-split-tune` and `landing-fixer-base-skills`, both failed at Darn-Write: the board stencil `darn-template-write` needs the `subagent_model` marker that `2d319fe5` added, and the old binary never fills it ("stencil: unfilled top-level marker(s): subagent_model").
The adopt check went green on the new tree, since it builds its own test binaries, so nothing flagged the stale install.

## Workaround

A run that landed on Neve right after the adopt ran the hub's deploy at its Land row, which installed a binary from the new `main`; the orch then resumed both darn runs at Darn-Write.
Had no run landed, the operator would have had to run `update-plugins.sh` by hand.

## Expected

- `lym adopt root` deploys when the adopted prime's `main` is ahead of the commit the installed binary was built from, running the hub's landing `deploy` command, the one `landing.yaml` names, before it lets any run go on.
- Short of that, adopt refuses to finish, or at least warns in its summary, when the installed binary predates the prime's `main`.

entries.title: Replay the landed plan-split tuning on both bench inputs and tune again
entries.body:
## Why

`plan-split-tune` landed the first round of tuning of the plan-split writers (Parts-Write, the part writers and the joining chair) without replaying it.
A replay must run the tuned lym and stencils, and stencils live only in the hub's shared Bolt copy, which takes only what lands on `main`, so the replays run here, after that landing, on the installed lym.

## Goal

Replay the landed tuning, then tune and replay again, until a split plan joins and passes its gates with no hand edit.
Start from the `plan-split-tune` report in `docs/research/` and the `plan-split-bench` report it builds on.

## Loop and cap

- Inputs: the two replays `plan-split-bench` used, `warp-visibility` (code at `d407ef69`, `_lym/discussion` and `_lym/reviews/discussion` from weft `576c4b3a31`) and `run-verbs-shared` (code at `52b69848`, the same directories from weft `b8a86e5c59`), each worktree with `plan_split: true` in its own `_lym/config/tapestry.yaml`.
- The first round replays the landed tuning with no further change.
- A later round tunes the instructions or gates, then replays Parts-Write and Parts-Plan-Write on both inputs.
- A tuning made in a later round reaches the replays only after it lands, so a later round that needs it ends this task with its change landed, and the report names what the next replay should check.
- Record per input and round whether the parts joined, which gates refused, and every hand edit needed.
- At most 2 rounds, so at most 4 split writings, and one Plan-Review round per input on the last round's plans only, 2 in all.
- The loop ends early at the first round where both inputs join and pass their gates with no hand edit.
- The orch creates and removes the scratch worktrees on the writer's request, since `lym fabric add` is refused from a task session.
- The results go into the same `docs/research/` report, round by round, with the cost.

entries.title: The sampler: code writer or read-only discussion role, and the skills that follow
entries.body:
## Question

Does the sampler stay a code writer, or become a read-only discussion role as note `discussed-task-split` proposes?

## What follows from the answer

- Skills: `internal/samplerengine/spec.go` gives the sampler `scribe:prose` and `scribe:conversation` only.
  As a code writer it needs `scribe:code-quality`, `scribe:testing` and the language skills, as every other code-writing seat lists, the same gap as task `landing-fixer-base-skills` closes for the landing fixer.
  As a read-only role, `scribe:prose` and `scribe:conversation` may be enough.
- PATTERN role: the directive itself is note `sampler-lacks-pattern-directive`; this answer only decides whether it is rendered for the implementer or the Discussion writer.
- Bundle with the other small sampler changes once the direction is settled.

## Also read (orch, 2026-11-02)

- Shell guard: the standing Bash denies of `internal/shellguard` render into every Claude session's settings through `internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine/settings.go`, the in-place edit row among them, so the sampler's session has them.
- Heddle: the batching rules reach a session through the worktree's rendered `CLAUDE.local.md`, so the sampler in its task worktree should have them; not verified in a live sampler session.
